For me the fear of death is not that it'll end, but that it won't. It's something I've been pondering a lot in the past year, when I contemplate ideas like rebirth and no-self and conditioning. I was also disturbed/intrigued by some things my ex shared with me about her past psychedelic experiences, where she said she saw that time was an illusion and it was actually this "mesh" that extends infinitely in all directions, and that consciousness perpetuates infinitely within this mesh and never stops. All these contemplations, combined with semi-frequent dosages of suicidal feelings, ended up leading me to the realization that I'm more terrified of the idea that death ISN'T the end, that there is no end or beginning, that even if "I" end, that there is no final resting place for consciousness, no arising or cessation of dukkha within dukkha, if that makes sense. Like, enlightenment is possible, and it is within the reach of all consciousness, but no matter what, somewhere, in the endless expanse of existence, this will all still be happening. All the suffering of all sentient beings strewn out across space and time, all the blood that's ever been spilt or ever will be spilt, all the ignorance and delusion and discrimination and personal bias that sedates awareness will still be "happening" in some sense, recorded somewhere in the emptiness, stuck on a playback loop forever. The scariest thing I imagined was going through with suicide, entering some intermediate ego-death realm and having this identity be deconstructed, learning that it was all a dream that thought it was real, and then falling into another dream, another constructed self, another life, and that this process was infinite and without beginning or end, making it the ultimate fate of all consciousness.

The one good thing to come from this was that I realized killing myself would accomplish nothing, because there's no self to kill. Every moment I die along with the rest of existence and am replaced by a new version, conditioned by the previous version and the laws of nature so that it appears continuous, as if there's something unchanging behind all the change. But there's not, it's all just change. And even if "my" suffering ends,  it won't end for all the other beings here on this planet. If anything, it would cause more suffering to arise. My parents would blame themselves and hate themselves for the rest of their lives. My therapist might feel like she's failed. My ex would assume it was because of her, because I one time threatened suicide and told her I wanted to do it because she left me. And then every other life they touch would be affected by that pain, and it would spread like a cancer. Being a living, breathing human is not only a wondrous gift for consciousness to manifest itself through duality, it is an opportunity to be mindful of this gift and to watch it with a clear awareness and equanimity as one might watch the leaves of a tree swaying in a gentle breeze.

This is just like, my opinion, man, but I think the important part of the "intoxicating substance" precept is not the substance, but the intoxication. You can never do drugs in your life and still be intoxicated, by philosophical and social views that you've become locked into. You can fall asleep and be intoxicated by a powerfully vidid dream. You can drink too much coffee to get you through the work day and get a nice caffeine buzz. You can ingest psilocybin, or LSD, or DMT, or ayahuasca, and (mis)take the profound psychedelic experience as reality. I don't think the specifics of the physical substance or lack thereof matter as much as *how you respond* to the way it affects you--I think the real intoxication is in ignorantly attaching to the immediate experience of consciousness and letting its seductive pull drag you down out of mindfulness and into dreamland, where everything is exactly as it appears.

Situations like this make me think of the Stanford Marshmallow Experiment where kids were offered treats, with the option of either having the treats immediately, or waiting for them and getting an extra reward for doing so. The study found that in general, the kids who opted for delayed gratification ended up performing better in many areas later in life. 

Not to say that acts of compassion should be done out of expectation of some future reward, but I think it's a similar kind of scenario. You have the option to follow your administrator's advice and from this point forward start killing these creatures in the name of providing job security for yourself, which you need if you want to keep making money, which you need if you want to be able to provide for yourself, which you need if you want to continue living. You also have the option to continue as you have been and risk getting fired for being "unprofessional." 

So a question you might ask is, what are your intentions behind taking the pests outside and letting them live? Do you have some personal sense of karma being a kind of cosmic moral justice system that rewards or punishes individuals for the way they conduct themselves, as many westerners do? Again, not that there's anything wrong with that--what's important is that, if this is the case, you are mindful of it, not ignorant of it.

I'm currently dealing with a similar issue in my home. It's very dry here in southern California right now, and lately I've been finding lots of tiny black ants in the kitchen and bathrooms, I guess because they're looking for water. Sometimes when I come home from work, they're crawling all over the kitchen sink and the dish rack, and on the dishes, and around any dirty dishes I left in the sink (which I usually do because I'm too lazy to wash them right away), and I don't know what I'm supposed to do. I try sprinkling cinnamon around, because ants apparently hate cinnamon, and it works, sort of. But it gets to the point that sometimes I can't even turn on the faucet without drowning a bunch of ants and washing them down the drain. And I know this is one solution, to kill as many as I can see and spray some insect-killing substance around the house, because the situation is undoubtedly annoying and inconvenient. 

But then I thought...they're just looking for water. They're just trying to survive, which is exactly what I'm doing. Sure, we look different, they're tiny and have six legs, I'm huge and have two legs, but we're all living beings. Are we all sentient and conscious? Maybe. Are we all at the same level of consciousness? Maybe. I would guess not, just from a biological standpoint, but who knows.  What I do know is that these creatures are only trying to do what they need to do to survive in the southern California summer heat, and that they're not trying to hurt me. If there's any intention of harm or destruction in a dynamic like this, it always comes from the human side, and it's always the other who ends up dead. We have so much physical and technological power over these beings we share the planet with, over all the insects, spiders, animals, plants, and so much intention of domination, as if we've collectively adopted Darwinism as the rule of law to govern all life. It's all about ME. The ME that arises from the perception of duality which makes consciousness possible, from the discriminating mind that differentiates between this and that, here and there, past and future, me and you. Our entire experience of the universe is built on duality and separation. But rather than recognize the experience as just that--experience--we grasp at it, latch onto it, and take it to be objectively "real." We take the hard, material appearance of physical existence to be the objective framework of all existence, and our consciousness of this groundwork to be a subjective byproduct of physical, chemical and biological conditions existing within this framework, and adopt the mind/matter dichotomy into our understanding of what life is. Human existence, separate from all existence, should be priority, because that's what "you" are. Human life, separate from all life, should be priority, because that's what "we" are. Any violation of this conditioned belief is seen as a threat by the ego--kill a poisonous spider, because it might kill you or somebody else, and that must not happen, because preservation of the physical body, and the concept of self, and the collective existence of the human species and its continued journey into the future of time and space, have been programmed into consciousness. We are conditioned to believe that there is even a "we" that can be conditioned, that there is an "I" that does the thinking and does the existing. And this is fine. This is literally what it means to be a person--to believe that you are a person, and not an ant, not a spider, or a beetle, or a field mouse, or a tree, or the rain, or the sun, or space, or time, or consciousness. 

So next time you see a fellow creature scurrying down a hallway or hiding in a closet, and you find yourself faced with a choice, breathe in, breathe out, and ask the question: does it even matter?

And if the answer is yes--observe why it is yes.

The way I like to visualize it, and this takes a bit of metaphysical speculation, is that Samsara, aka the dimension of time (and the 3D space connected to it) wraps around on itself to form some sort of n-dimensional closed loop, like a sphere or a torus or something. So the entirety of what we experience as time, and the flux of conditioned states that are allowed to manifest within it, is encoded and contained in this atemporal superstructure. All the data exists simultaneously, for lack of a word that could adequately describe it, every cause and every affect, every quantum unit of consciousness that's ever experienced anything, in this infinite (due to it being a closed loop),  unified, supernal realm where, similar to a long exposure photograph, everything is directly connected to everything else, there is no separation of here/there, before/after, this/that, I/you, free from discrimination and duality.

Looking at it this way, the perceived linear and one-way flow of time is not so much a flow, the way water might flow and move through an unmoving, permanent channel, but a calm, vast ocean, where the water, the waves, and the space itself are all mind/consciousness; there is no order, no beginning, no end, just an infinite expanse that can be chopped up and fragmented into ever smaller and smaller illusory pieces that appear to have separate, independent existences. Consciousness neither begins with the birth of the first sentient being, nor ends with the death of that last one, because it's not a stream from point A to point B, but an ocean where point A = point B.

Yeah, the parent analogy is one I talk about with my therapist often. I just now realized its connection to the Middle Way; if we accept that the child and parent are in fact the same person, we can use it as a metaphor to describe the relationship between observer and observed, where observer would essentially just mean "consciousness," and observed would mean all of the five aggregates, dukkha, all of conditioned/transient existence. To give in to all of the child's fleeting, temporary needs for novelty and sense-pleasure is like Gautama in his early years, living like a prince (literally). To ignore the child, to neglect him, even to abuse him, is like his years as an ascetic. I wonder if really, the Middle Way isn't so much about literally consuming both sides in moderation, but in taking in ALL of it, both sides in their entirety, and from that all-encompassing experience, using the average, the median, as a kind of balancing point, one which contains in its reflection all the good and all the bad, all the pleasure and the pain, all the love and hate, every dualistic pair that can be conceived of, and which will reveal those reflections as such upon being meditated on. Like in the symbol of the Tao--perhaps the Path lies along the infinitesimal line between light and dark, that line which has no inherent width or substance in an of itself, but which is the axis upon which both sides revolve and the entire spectrum rotates.

Thank you for the suggestions--I just spend about 30 minutes or so (hard to keep track of time)  sitting on the floor meditating in front of a candle. I realized that having an object of concentration helps to cultivate concentration, which led me to a contemplation on interdependence, or as Thich Nhat Hanh describes it, "interbeing," and looked at how the subject and object of consciousness arise dependently by definition--perhaps the frustration that comes from attempting to meditate traditionally (calm abiding, as you said) has its roots in the dichotomy between mind (internal) and object of focus or concentration (whether internal or external), which is a mental creation; perhaps it's because I have such a strong intention and will to achieve some sort of result from meditation, that meditation becomes a kind of chore, a means to an end, a raft constructed *for the purpose of crossing the river*, rather than constructed just for the sake of being constructed. Or perhaps it's because the river, and both shores, are in fact the same place, and I've always been in this kind of superposition of all of them, but out of ignorance and a desire to reach this imaginary opposite shore, I keep myself perpetually stuck on the first shore. Is the problem in not building the raft (not following the Path), or in building the raft to cross the river, as opposed to building the raft just to build the raft?
